01 Accumulation & Wealth Building

The Money Illusion

Why a 7% return can still leave you poorer — and how to find the one number that tells you the truth.

The Planning LetterReal vs. Nominal Returns

Picture two savers at a dinner party. The first leans back and announces that her portfolio returned 7% last year. The second, quieter, mentions he keeps most of his money in a high-yield savings account paying a comfortable 4%. Both feel they are winning. Both are describing a mirage.

The number printed on a statement — the one we quote at parties — is the nominal return. It is the return measured in dollars, and dollars are a ruler that shrinks a little every year. Inflation is the quiet tax that no one votes for, charged not at the register but on the value of every dollar you already hold. The only figure that describes whether your wealth actually grew is the real return: what's left after inflation has taken its cut.

Most of personal finance is taught in nominal terms because nominal numbers are bigger, and bigger feels better. This letter is an argument for unlearning that habit. Once you see returns in real terms, a great deal of conventional advice rearranges itself — and the "safe" money becomes the most quietly dangerous money you own.

The Mechanism

The Fisher Effect, in plain English

The instinct is to subtract: 7% return minus 3% inflation equals 4% real. That's close, but it's lazy arithmetic, and the gap matters once you compound it over decades. The economist Irving Fisher gave us the precise version. Real return isn't subtraction; it's division, because you're deflating the whole grown balance by the whole year of price increases.

real = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1
real = (1.07) ÷ (1.03) − 1 = 3.88%
The lazy subtraction gives 4.00%. Fisher gives 3.88%. That 0.12% wedge is small in one year and brutal across thirty — it's the difference between a number you celebrate and a number that's true.

So our first saver's 7% is really 3.88%. Her purchasing power — her ability to buy groceries, plane tickets, and a roof — grew by less than four cents on the dollar. Respectable, but only half the story she told at dinner.

Now turn to the second saver, the cautious one. His 4% savings account, against the same 3% inflation, returns a real 0.97%. And in years when inflation runs hot — as it did in 2022 — that same "safe" account can post a deeply negative real return. Safety from market swings is not the same as safety from erosion.

"Safe" money doesn't fail loudly. It fails silently, on schedule, every single year.

What You Keep

Then the tax man arrives

Inflation isn't the only claim on your return. In a taxable account, the IRS taxes your nominal gain — it does not give you a discount for the part that was merely keeping pace with inflation. You can pay real tax on a phantom gain. Stack the two forces and the headline 7% thins out considerably.

The Practical Number

Your hurdle rate: the minimum that isn't losing

Here is the one calculation worth committing to memory. Your hurdle rate is the nominal return you must earn just to break even — to stand still in real, after-tax terms. Earn less than your hurdle, and despite a positive statement, you are moving backward. The formula is mercifully simple:

hurdle = inflation ÷ (1 − your tax rate)
At 3% inflation and a 24% bracket: 0.03 ÷ 0.76 = 3.95%. Below that, you're not earning — you're slowly liquidating.

Notice what this reframes. The "high-yield" cash account paying 4% clears a Roth hurdle but barely clears a taxable one. The point is not to abandon cash — every plan needs liquidity — but to stop mistaking a slow leak for a safe harbor. Cash is a tool for spending soon, not for growing over decades.

Today's Move

Calculate your real hurdle rate

Five minutes, one number. Once you know it, every account you own can be judged honestly.

  1. Pick an inflation assumption. The long-run U.S. average is ~3%. Use that unless you have reason to expect more.
  2. Find your marginal tax rate on each account's gains: 0% for Roth, your capital-gains rate for long-held taxable positions, your ordinary bracket for interest and short-term gains.
  3. Divide inflation by (1 minus that rate). That's the hurdle for that account.
  4. Hold each account's actual yield up against its hurdle. Anything earning less than its hurdle is losing real value — flag it.
  5. For any flagged dollar you won't spend within ~2 years, ask whether it belongs somewhere with a fighting chance against the hurdle.

The money illusion is seductive because it flatters us. Nominal numbers are always bigger; they always feel like progress. But wealth is not measured in dollars — it's measured in what those dollars command. Learn to see in real terms, and you'll never again be fooled by a number that grew while your life got smaller.

Next week, we move from how much you keep to where you should put the next dollar you save — and why the order matters more than the amount.
